label: Continuity As Topological Control
notes: Begin by positioning continuity as a way to control tests on the target space, not as a picture of a smooth graph. The important reversal is contravariant: an open set in the codomain becomes a diagnostic subset of the domain. This framing prepares every later example in the chapter, including restrictions, seam failures, space-filling limits, and metric extensions.

label: Neighborhoods To Open Sets
notes: Use this slide to rebuild the chapter's first equivalence. A neighborhood can be larger than the actual room around a point, but it must contain some open witness. Once open sets are adopted as primitive, the topology is easier to manipulate because unions and finite intersections are global rules rather than point-by-point bookkeeping.

label: Subspace And Discrete Topologies
notes: Emphasize that subspace topology changes which points are allowed to test nearby behavior. The same drawn component may look like it has a boundary in the plane, yet inside the subspace the missing middle gap is unavailable. That is why the notebook check records the right component as both open and closed in the induced topology.

label: Closed Sets And Limit Points
notes: Treat closedness as a promise about forced points. The set of points 1 over n illustrates the distinction between belonging to a set and being forced by nearby samples. The theorem says that a closed set has already accepted all such forced points, while a nonclosed set can be detected by a limit point left outside.

label: Closure Interior Frontier
notes: Use the table as a compact decision record rather than a list to memorize. The point is to compare three questions: what is safely inside, what is forced by closure, and what is touched from both sides. The clopen subspace row is especially useful because it shows the frontier can disappear when the ambient middle is removed.

label: Bases Local Tests
notes: Present a base as a smaller test kit. Instead of checking every possible open set directly, one verifies that basic opens refine neighborhoods and behave well under finite intersections. This is the practical entry point for the continuity theorem, because target bases let us test fewer inverse images without changing the topology.

label: Preimage Continuity
notes: Focus attention on the direction of inverse images. The target band is drawn in the codomain, but the answer to continuity lives in the domain. The square map creates two open intervals, while the jump map traps an endpoint. That endpoint is the whole obstruction, and it is enough to reject continuity.

label: Equivalent Continuity Tests
notes: The implication graph is a theorem map, not a dependency graph for code alone. Its value is that it lets an instructor choose the most convenient continuity test for the situation. Base tests are efficient, closed-set tests are often simpler in metric spaces, and closure tests explain why limit behavior is preserved.

label: Composition And Restriction
notes: Composition and restriction are bookkeeping, but they are important bookkeeping. For composition, the target open set is pulled back through g and then through f. For restriction, the same preimage is simply intersected with the subspace. Both arguments teach students to trust inverse images as the algebraic engine behind continuous maps.

label: Continuous Bijection Failure
notes: The circle example separates continuous bijection from homeomorphism. The forward map passes the base-open test, including arcs crossing the seam, because the subspace topology on the interval makes the split preimage open. The inverse fails because points approaching the seam on the circle can correspond to parameters approaching one, while the seam itself is assigned parameter zero.

label: Homeomorphism And Stereographic Projection
notes: Stereographic projection gives the positive model after the circle warning. Here the geometry supplies both directions: project from the missing pole to the plane, and recover a point of the sphere by reversing the same line. The proof is still topological, because open target sets pull back through the family of half-lines to subspace-open sets.

label: Disc Boundary Moves
notes: These disc lemmas are included because continuity becomes usable in surgery arguments. A boundary map can be pushed inward along radial segments, which is a controlled homeomorphism of the full disc. The second lemma uses that extension idea twice to replace two discs sharing an arc by one standard disc.

label: Space Filling Curve
notes: Frame space filling as uniform approximation rather than a visual paradox. The finite stages do not yet fill the square, but each stage gives a concrete covering guarantee. The table matters because it records how the maximum distance from any point of the square to the finite path decreases stage by stage.

label: Uniform Approximation
notes: Use the numerical table to slow down the word uniform. Pointwise closeness would not be enough for the argument in the source span. What matters is one bound that works for every parameter value at once. The chapter then postpones the final onto conclusion until compactness proves that the limiting image is closed.

label: Metric Separation
notes: Distances to closed sets are continuous numerical sensors. Once two closed sets are disjoint, the sum of their distances cannot vanish, so the normalized difference gives a separator. This slide should connect the geometric picture to the algebraic formula, because that formula is the engine used repeatedly inside the Tietze proof.

label: Tietze Roadmap
notes: End by turning Tietze into an algorithmic proof roadmap. The construction does not guess the extension at once. It repeatedly separates two closed error sets, adds a bounded correction, and makes the remaining error smaller by a fixed factor. Uniform convergence then makes the infinite correction a continuous function on the whole space.
